## Analysis

The diff changes `parseRegExp` from `/^((-|\+)?(\d+(?:\.\d+)?)) *(kb|mb|gb|tb|pb)$/i` to `/^((-|\+)?(\d(?:\.\d+)?)) *(kb|mb|gb|tb|pb)$/i` — it drops the `+` quantifier from the integer part of the number. The new regex only matches values with a **single digit** before the (optional) decimal point.

Consequence: any multi-digit value with a unit, e.g. `'100kb'`, `'1024mb'`, `'-100kb'`, no longer matches `parseRegExp`. In `parse()`, `results` is `null`, so the code takes the fallback branch:

```javascript
floatValue = parseInt(val, 10);
unit = 'b';
```

which parses only the leading digits and **silently discards the unit**, treating the value as plain bytes. So `bytes.parse('100kb')` returns `100` instead of `102400`, and `bytes.parse('-100kb')` returns `-100` instead of `-102400`. (Single-digit values like `'1kb'`/`'1.5kb'` still match, which is why the library's own suite stays green.)

```json
{"defect": true, "testFile": {"path": "test/proof-test.js", "content": "'use strict';\n\nvar assert = require('assert');\nvar bytes = require('..');\n\ndescribe('proof', function () {\n  it('fails on the patched build', function () {\n    // multi-digit values with a unit must be parsed with the unit applied\n    assert.strictEqual(bytes('100kb'), 102400);\n    assert.strictEqual(bytes('10kb'), 10240);\n    assert.strictEqual(bytes.parse('1024mb'), 1073741824);\n    assert.strictEqual(bytes.parse('-100kb'), -102400);\n  });\n});\n"}, "note": "Removing '+' from parseRegExp restricts matches to single-digit integer parts, so inputs like '100kb' no longer match the regex and fall into the parseInt(val, 10) fallback, which ignores the unit and returns 100 instead of 102400 (signed values like '-100kb' return -100 instead of -102400)."}
```
